query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Trace carbon doping (approximately 0.1 at.%) in a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) such as Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 will induce the formation of fine, stable carbide precipitates at high temperatures that impede dislocation motion, thereby improving high-temperature yield strength by roughly 10–20% compared to the undoped alloy, while leaving room‐temperature strength, ductility, and overall density essentially unchanged.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy in the Mo–Nb–Re–Ta–W family with well‐characterized room-temperature strength and ductility but limited high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace amount of carbon (ca. 0.1 at.%) to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy is subjected to service conditions typical of jet-turbine applications, i.e., high temperatures (for example, 800–1200 °C) during mechanical loading while still requiring good room-temperature performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of fine carbide precipitates (e.g., Ta3C or Nb3C) during high-temperature service.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the minor carbon addition precipitates as stable carbides that act as obstacles to dislocation motion (precipitation strengthening), enhancing high-temperature yield strength; meanwhile, at room temperature the low level of carbon does not alter the alloy’s solid solution phase or its density significantly, thus preserving its mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement of high-temperature yield strength by approximately 10–20% over the undoped baseline, with negligible change in room-temperature mechanical performance and overall alloy density.
generation.baseline: The undoped refractory high-entropy alloy with documented high-temperature strength (e.g., yield strength of around 405 MPa at 1600 °C for some RHEAs) and acceptable room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected as long as carbon remains a trace addition (around 0.1 at.%) and the processing conditions allow for the controlled formation of carbides during high-temperature exposure. Excess carbon or different processing routes may lead to unwanted phase formation or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics and stability of carbide precipitation at service temperatures and the quantitative improvement in yield strength depend on subtle processing variables and thermal histories that have not been fully established yet.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the selected RHEA alloy: one set with 0.1 at.% carbon added and one set without carbon. Subject both sets to identical thermomechanical processing and then perform tensile tests at both room temperature and at high temperatures (e.g., 800–1200 °C). Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to analyze the microstructure for the presence of fine carbide precipitates in the carbon-doped samples.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant (approximately >10%) improvement in high-temperature yield strength relative to the undoped alloy, or if room-temperature properties (strength or ductility) are adversely affected, or if the expected carbide precipitates are absent under high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.
